analysis.one_liner: Charges fossil fuel producers a rising fee per ton of carbon and returns the money to Americans as monthly dividends.
analysis.headline: The carbon fee and dividend bill never received a hearing or vote in any House committee and died when the 118th Congress ended, despite 33 House cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would charge oil, gas, and coal producers and importers a fee for every ton of carbon their fuels will emit, starting at $15 per ton and rising $10 each year. Nearly all of the money would flow into a Carbon Dividend Trust Fund and be paid out monthly to every U.S. citizen and lawful resident — one full share per adult, half per child. It also puts matching fees on carbon-intensive imports and refunds the fee on exports, to keep U.S. manufacturers from being undercut by countries without carbon rules.
analysis.who_benefits: Most citizens and lawful residents would receive monthly dividend payments from the new trust fund. Because the fee is collected from fuel producers upstream and the dividend is the same for everyone, households that use less energy than average — typically lower- and middle-income families — would generally come out ahead financially even though fuel prices rise. The bill also gives refunds to facilities that capture and store carbon dioxide and protects energy-intensive manufacturers like steel and cement from carbon-intensive imports.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a fee on covered fuels starting at $15 per metric ton of CO2-e in 2023 and rising $10 per year, with an even larger increase if emissions miss the annual reduction target.

Requires nearly all fee revenue to go into a Carbon Dividend Trust Fund for monthly payments to every eligible U.S. citizen or lawful resident, one share per adult and half a share per child under 19.
Specifies that carbon dividends do not count as income or resources for determining eligibility for any federal or federally assisted benefit program.
Exempts fuels used on farms and by the Armed Forces, and pays refunds to facilities that capture and permanently sequester carbon dioxide.

Adds border fee adjustments — fees on carbon-intensive imports and refunds on exports — so foreign producers without carbon pricing cannot undercut U.S. manufacturers, and routes some of that revenue to the Green Climate Fund.

analysis.who_pays: Producers and importers of crude oil, natural gas, and coal pay the fee, and those costs are expected to be passed through to consumers in gasoline, heating, and electricity prices. Households that drive long distances or heat with fossil fuels could pay more than they receive in dividends. Dividend payments count as taxable gross income, which trims the net benefit, and the escalating fee raises energy costs further every year until emissions fall below 10% of 2005 levels.
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers and heavy energy users

drawbacks.text: The fee is collected from producers and importers of crude oil, natural gas, and coal, and those costs would be passed through to consumers at the pump and in utility bills — an unavoidable feature of any carbon price.
Dividend payments are includible in gross income, so the after-tax net benefit is smaller than the headline check for households owing income tax.

The fee escalates by $10 per metric ton every year with no cap until emissions fall below 10% of 2005 levels and dividends fall under $20 a month, so energy prices would keep climbing for decades under the bill's schedule.

The dividend is universal rather than means-tested, so high-energy-use households — long-distance drivers, households heating with fuel oil — could pay more in higher fuel costs than they receive back.
Facilities with carbon capture equipment receive refund payments equal to the fee on fuel they use, directing a share of the program's money back to industrial operations.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The design is deliberately progressive: an identical dividend to every resident offsets higher fuel costs for most lower- and middle-income households, while higher prices fall hardest on the heaviest energy users and on fossil fuel producers. The honest costs are real — energy prices rise every year under the bill's schedule, the dividend is taxed as income, and the climate result depends entirely on the fee climbing as written rather than being watered down later. Versions of this carbon-fee-and-dividend approach have been introduced repeatedly and have never advanced in Congress, largely because the fee is a direct, escalating cost to a powerful fuel industry and the revenue goes to households rather than to government programs or industry.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in three House committees — Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Foreign Affairs — for the rest of the Congress without a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and expired when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Salud Carbajal introduced the bill on September 27, 2023, joined by Rep. Scott Peters, and it was referred to the Committees on Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Foreign Affairs.
It was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy, Climate and Grid Security on September 29, 2023, and later to subcommittees on Social Security and Trade in December 2024.
Thirty-two House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republican did.
No committee reported the bill, no hearing or markup was held, and no floor vote ever occurred before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fossil fuel producers and importers are better off because no carbon fee was ever imposed, and no household ever received the dividends the bill promised. Status quo energy pricing, and the emissions trajectory that goes with it, continued.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Fossil fuel producers avoided the fee

sides.party_line_note: All 33 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and with Republicans holding a 224-seat House majority the bill never advanced in any committee.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and refiners
industries.note: Refineries, natural gas pipeline operators, and fuel importers would pay the carbon fee on every ton their fuels emit, starting at $15 and rising $10 per year. The fee is the funding source for the household dividends, so the industry's interest in blocking it runs directly against the payments to citizens.

Coal mining operations and coal importers are covered entities liable for the fee on the greenhouse gas content of their coal. The escalating rate would raise coal's cost faster than competitors without carbon pricing.
By making fossil fuels progressively more expensive, the fee shifts demand toward non-emitting energy sources. Clean power providers gain market ground without a direct subsidy.

Industrial facilities that capture and permanently sequester carbon dioxide from fee-covered fuels receive refund payments equal to the fee, effectively subsidizing capture technology. It is a direct revenue channel for the capture industry.

industries.industry: Energy-intensive manufacturers (steel, cement, aluminum, chemicals, glass, paper)
industries.note: These industries pay more for fossil fuel energy under the fee, but the bill's border provisions charge matching fees on carbon-intensive imports and refund fees on exports, shielding them from competition from countries without carbon pricing. Their interest in the bill runs alongside the public's interest in preventing emissions from simply moving overseas.
